  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Analysis of ICSID tribunals in claims against Argentina}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%",
                      dpi = 150)
library(hypergraphs)
comma <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
num <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
day <- function(x) trimws(format(x, "%e %B %Y"))
```

```{r ranking, include = FALSE}
case_states <- unique(subset(icsid_tribunals, select = c(case, respondent)))
claims <- aggregate(case ~ respondent, data = case_states, FUN = length)
argentina_claims <- subset(claims, respondent == "Argentine Republic")$case
argentina_rank <- sum(claims$case > argentina_claims) + 1L
rank_word <- switch(argentina_rank, "largest", "second-largest",
                    "third-largest")
```

This case study examines tribunal membership in ICSID claims against
the Argentine Republic. In the released `icsid_tribunals` data,
`r argentina_claims` of `r comma(nrow(case_states))` cases concern
Argentina, the `r rank_word` count among respondent states. Arbitrators
are represented as nodes and three-member tribunals as hyperedges.
Constitution and conclusion dates define the recorded observation interval
for each tribunal.

The tutorial describes appointment concentration, repeated panels,
concurrent connectivity, hyperedge centrality, and communities. It also
compares these observations with cases against other states in the same
release. The hypergraph retains complete tribunal membership; temporal
snapshots distinguish concurrent appointments from relationships visible
only after aggregation. The analysis concerns recorded membership
structure and does not estimate appointment mechanisms or case outcomes.

## Data

Select records whose respondent is Argentina. Each retained row
identifies one tribunal seat. Keep case identifiers and dates available
so that repeated panels and overlapping observation intervals can be
examined separately.

```{r data}
argentina <- subset(icsid_tribunals, respondent == "Argentine Republic")
```

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_cases <- length(unique(argentina$case))
n_arbitrators <- length(unique(argentina$arbitrator))
n_pending <- length(unique(subset(argentina, !is_concluded)$case))
case_dates <- unique(subset(argentina, select = c(case, constituted)))
origin_date <- min(case_dates$constituted)
end_offset <- as.numeric(as.Date("2023-06-15") - origin_date)
first_tribunal <- format(origin_date, "%Y")
last_tribunal <- format(max(case_dates$constituted), "%Y")
early <- nrow(subset(case_dates, constituted < as.Date("2006-01-01")))
wave <- nrow(subset(case_dates, constituted >= as.Date("2003-01-01") &
                      constituted < as.Date("2005-01-01")))
dated_pending <- unique(subset(argentina, !is_concluded & !is.na(concluded),
                               select = c(case, concluded)))
year_of <- function(t) format(origin_date + t, "%Y")
```

The subset contains `r n_cases` cases and `r n_arbitrators` arbitrators.
Tribunal constitution dates range from `r first_tribunal` to
`r last_tribunal`; `r early` tribunals were constituted before 2006,
including `r wave` in 2003–2004. At the observation endpoint of
15 June 2023, `r n_pending` cases have a pending status. One of them,
`r dated_pending$case`, also has a conclusion date of
`r day(dated_pending$concluded)`. The temporal construction uses that
recorded date as its endpoint. This data inconsistency is retained
explicitly rather than resolved through the status label.

## The temporal hypergraph

Use interval construction with arbitrator identifiers as `node`, case
identifiers as `hyperedge`, and the constitution and conclusion columns
as the clock. Missing conclusion dates remain open through
`observation_end`. Case-level constants, including economic sector, are
stored as hyperedge attributes. Construct comparable objects for all
ICSID cases and for cases against states other than Argentina.

```{r build}
tribunals <- temporal_hypergraph(argentina, node = "arbitrator",
                                 hyperedge = "case", start = "constituted",
                                 end = "concluded",
                                 observation_end = as.Date("2023-06-15"))
summary(tribunals)
all_tribunals <- temporal_hypergraph(icsid_tribunals, node = "arbitrator",
                                     hyperedge = "case", start = "constituted",
                                     end = "concluded",
                                     observation_end = as.Date("2023-06-15"))
others <- subset(icsid_tribunals, respondent != "Argentine Republic")
other_tribunals <- temporal_hypergraph(others, node = "arbitrator",
                                       hyperedge = "case", start = "constituted",
                                       end = "concluded",
                                       observation_end = as.Date("2023-06-15"))
```

```{r build-values, include = FALSE}
mean_years <- summary(tribunals)$mean_duration / 365.25
```

The mean observed interval for the Argentina subset is
`r num(mean_years, 1)` years. This includes intervals bounded by the
observation endpoint and therefore differs from completed-case duration.
The endpoint cumulative snapshot contains all tribunals in the subset.
Its multi-hypergraph (`mh`) retains each observation, while its binary
hypergraph (`bh`) retains each distinct panel once. The clique projection
either counts all pair occurrences (`mg`) or retains distinct pairs
only (`bg`).

```{r representations}
argentina_all <- hg_snapshot(tribunals, mode = "cumulative")
icsid_all <- hg_snapshot(all_tribunals, mode = "cumulative")
others_all <- hg_snapshot(other_tribunals, mode = "cumulative")
hg_representations(argentina_all)
```

```{r representations-values, include = FALSE}
reps <- hg_representations(argentina_all)
other_reps <- hg_representations(others_all)
rep_value <- function(r, col, x = reps) unlist(subset(x, representation == r, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
repeat_share <- (rep_value("mh", "n_edges") - rep_value("bh", "n_edges")) /
  rep_value("mh", "n_edges")
other_repeat_share <- (rep_value("mh", "n_edges", other_reps) -
                         rep_value("bh", "n_edges", other_reps)) /
  rep_value("mh", "n_edges", other_reps)
```

The `r rep_value("mh", "n_edges")` tribunals contribute
`r rep_value("mg", "n_edges")` pair occurrences and
`r rep_value("bg", "n_edges")` distinct arbitrator pairs. The pairwise
projection cannot recover which three pairs belong to the same tribunal.
There are `r rep_value("bh", "n_edges")` distinct panels, so repeated
observations beyond the first occurrence account for
`r pct(repeat_share)` of tribunals. The corresponding share for cases
against other states is `r pct(other_repeat_share)`. This comparison
describes repetition in two differently sized sets of observations.

## Who decided the claims

The incidence plot places arbitrators in rows and tribunals in
columns. Each column marks its three members. Rows are ordered by
tribunal count and columns by constitution date. Colour and shape encode
economic sector, permitting membership structure to be read alongside
case attributes.

```{r incidence, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 13}
plot(argentina_all, type = "incidence", color_by = "economic_sector",
     sort_by = "start", edge_labels = TRUE,
     legend_title = "economic sector")
```

```{r incidence-values, include = FALSE}
panels <- aggregate(arbitrator ~ case + constituted, data = argentina,
                    FUN = \(a) paste(sort(a), collapse = " | "))
repeated <- subset(panels, duplicated(arbitrator) |
                     duplicated(arbitrator, fromLast = TRUE))
pairs <- aggregate(case ~ arbitrator, data = repeated,
                   FUN = \(x) paste(sort(x), collapse = " and "))
same_day <- aggregate(constituted ~ arbitrator, data = repeated,
                      FUN = \(d) length(unique(d)) == 1L)
repeat_years <- sort(unique(format(repeated$constituted, "%Y")))
busiest <- subset(hg_get(argentina_all, what = "nodes"), degree >= 4)
busiest_seats <- subset(argentina, arbitrator %in% busiest$node)
busiest_early <- mean(busiest_seats$constituted < as.Date("2006-01-01"))
```

An identical panel produces another column with marks in the same
three rows. The `r nrow(pairs)` repeated-panel pairs are
`r paste(pairs$case, collapse = ", ")`. They were constituted in
`r paste(repeat_years, collapse = " and ")`; `r sum(same_day$constituted)`
pairs share a constitution date. Of the seats held by arbitrators with
at least four appointments, `r pct(busiest_early)` belong to tribunals
constituted before 2006. These temporal details are important when
interpreting repetition as a sequence of appointments.

Hyperdegree counts an arbitrator's tribunals. Binary clique degree
counts distinct colleagues across those tribunals. An arbitrator can
therefore have a large appointment count while working repeatedly with
a relatively small set of colleagues.

```{r degrees}
hg_get(argentina_all, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree", top = 5)
tribunal_counts <- hg_measures(argentina_all, what = "distribution",
                               measure = "hyperdegree")
colleague_counts <- hg_measures(argentina_all, what = "distribution",
                                measure = "n_neighbors")
```

```{r degrees-values, include = FALSE}
one_tribunal <- 1 - subset(tribunal_counts, value == 2)$ccdf
top_arbitrator <- hg_get(argentina_all, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree",
                         top = 1)
top_share <- function(h) {
  degrees <- hg_get(h, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree")$degree
  sum(head(degrees, 10L)) / sum(degrees)
}
argentina_top <- top_share(argentina_all)
other_top <- top_share(others_all)
max_colleagues <- max(colleague_counts$value)
```

The complementary cumulative curves give the proportion of
arbitrators with at least each tribunal count or colleague count.

```{r degrees-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(tribunal_counts)
plot(colleague_counts)
```

In this subset, `r pct(one_tribunal)` of arbitrators appear on one
tribunal. `r top_arbitrator$node` has `r top_arbitrator$degree` tribunal
memberships, and the largest colleague count is `r max_colleagues`.
The ten most frequently appointed arbitrators constitute
`r pct(10 / n_arbitrators)` of arbitrators and hold
`r pct(argentina_top)` of seats. The corresponding ten-person seat share
for cases against other states is `r pct(other_top)`.
This is a descriptive concentration measure, whose denominator depends
on the number of cases and arbitrators in each subset.

Degree assortativity describes whether frequently appointed
arbitrators tend to share tribunals. The uniform choice function selects
a pair of distinct members within each tribunal, and the measure
correlates their degree ranks over that pair distribution. The function
calculates the expected coefficient directly rather than simulating
one pair per tribunal. This is a generalised Spearman-type measure
(Chodrow 2020).

```{r assortativity}
hg_assortativity(argentina_all)
hg_assortativity(others_all)
```

```{r assortativity-values, include = FALSE}
assort_argentina <- hg_assortativity(argentina_all)$assortativity
assort_other <- hg_assortativity(others_all)$assortativity
```

The rank assortativity coefficients are `r num(assort_argentina)`
for Argentina cases and `r num(assort_other)` for the other cases.
Positive values describe assortative mixing by appointment frequency.
The difference between these coefficients is descriptive; no test of
the between-subset difference has been specified here.

## Repeated panels

Two repetition statistics count additional joint appearances.
`repeated_pairs` is the number of pair occurrences minus the number of
distinct pairs. `repeated_edges` is the number of tribunals minus the
number of distinct panels. Both retain multiplicity beyond the first
appearance of a pair or panel.

Compare them under two null models, each using 999 draws. The swap model
preserves node hyperdegrees and tribunal sizes through checkerboard
swaps (Gotelli 2000). The assignment model processes arbitrators in
decreasing hyperdegree and assigns them to free tribunal seats
(Coupette et al. 2024). Successful assignment draws preserve the same
margins, but the two algorithms define different reference distributions.

```{r repeats}
repeats_swap <- hg_null_test(argentina_all,
                             statistic = c("repeated_pairs", "repeated_edges"),
                             method = "swap", n = 999, seed = 1)
repeats_swap
repeats_assignment <- hg_null_test(argentina_all,
                                   statistic = c("repeated_pairs", "repeated_edges"),
                                   method = "assignment", n = 999, seed = 1)
repeats_assignment
```

Repeat the swap-model calculation on all ICSID tribunals and on the
subset excluding Argentina. This examines how the observed departure
changes when the subset is removed; it is not a formal test comparing
the two groups' effects.

```{r repeats-icsid}
repeats_icsid <- hg_null_test(icsid_all,
                              statistic = c("repeated_pairs", "repeated_edges"),
                              method = "swap", n = 999, seed = 1)
repeats_icsid
repeats_other <- hg_null_test(others_all,
                              statistic = c("repeated_pairs", "repeated_edges"),
                              method = "swap", n = 999, seed = 1)
repeats_other
```

```{r repeats-values, include = FALSE}
test_value <- function(x, s, col) unlist(subset(x, statistic == s, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

For Argentina cases, the additional pair count is
`r test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_pairs", "observed")`, with a
central 95% swap-null interval from
`r test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_pairs", "null_lo")` to
`r test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_pairs", "null_hi")` and a
standardised deviation of
`r num(test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_pairs", "z"), 1)`.
The additional panel count is
`r test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_edges", "observed")`, with interval
`r test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_edges", "null_lo")` to
`r test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_edges", "null_hi")`, z-score
`r num(test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_edges", "z"), 1)`, and p-value
`r num(test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_edges", "p_value"), 3)`.

Under the assignment model, the z-scores are
`r num(test_value(repeats_assignment, "repeated_pairs", "z"), 1)` for
pairs and `r num(test_value(repeats_assignment, "repeated_edges", "z"), 1)`
for panels. For all ICSID tribunals, the corresponding swap-model
z-scores are `r num(test_value(repeats_icsid, "repeated_pairs", "z"), 1)`
and `r num(test_value(repeats_icsid, "repeated_edges", "z"), 1)`.
After excluding Argentina, p-values are
`r num(test_value(repeats_other, "repeated_pairs", "p_value"), 2)` and
`r num(test_value(repeats_other, "repeated_edges", "p_value"), 2)`.
Interpret these results conditional on each subset's margins and the
chosen randomisation. A change in statistical significance across
subsets does not itself establish a significant difference between them.

## Motifs

The motif census evaluates induced configurations on four arbitrators.
Y, T, and O contain exactly two, three, and four distinct three-member
tribunals, respectively. Duplicate panels are collapsed before counting.
The configuration randomisation preserves degrees and edge sizes during
member exchanges, followed by duplicate collapse for the simple-graph
census. The aggregate comparison uses 1,000 draws.

```{r motifs}
motifs <- hg_motifs(argentina_all, n = 1000, seed = 1)
motifs
```

```{r motifs-values, include = FALSE}
motif_row <- function(x, m, col) unlist(subset(x, motif == m, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

```{r motifs-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(motifs)
```

The aggregate has `r motif_row(motifs, "Y", "count")` Y configurations,
with null mean `r num(motif_row(motifs, "Y", "expected"), 1)`, z-score
`r num(motif_row(motifs, "Y", "z"), 1)`, and p-value
`r num(motif_row(motifs, "Y", "p_value"), 3)`.
Aggregation can combine tribunals with non-overlapping case intervals.
The next calculation therefore repeats the census on annual snapshots,
which include only tribunals active together at those measurement times.

```{r motifs-time}
years <- seq(as.Date("2003-01-01"), as.Date("2015-01-01"), by = "year")
yearly_motifs <- hg_motifs(tribunals, n = 300, seed = 1, at = years)
subset(yearly_motifs, motif == "Y",
       select = c(time, count, expected, z, p_value))
```

```{r motifs-time-values, include = FALSE}
yearly_y <- subset(yearly_motifs, motif == "Y")
max_y <- max(yearly_y$count)
min_p <- min(yearly_y$p_value)
```

The largest annual-snapshot Y count is `r max_y`, and the smallest
snapshot p-value is `r num(min_p, 2)`. The evidence from these snapshots
differs from that of the aggregate. The snapshots have smaller counts
and address concurrent structure; absence of a small p-value is not
evidence that concurrent structure is random.

## How the docket changed

Measure the active tribunal and arbitrator counts on 1 January of
each year from 2002 to 2022. Columns ending in `_cumulative` describe
everything observed by that date. With `components = TRUE`, the result
also reports concurrent component count, the largest component's node
share, and its diameter. This is a sequence of static snapshots, not a
model of time-ordered movement through cases.

```{r growth}
grid <- seq(as.Date("2002-01-01"), as.Date("2022-01-01"), by = "year")
docket <- hg_growth(tribunals, components = TRUE, at = grid)
tail(docket, 3)
```

```{r growth-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(docket,
     columns = c("n_nodes", "n_edges", "n_nodes_cumulative",
                 "n_edges_cumulative"),
     facets = FALSE)
plot(docket, columns = c("n_components", "diameter"), facets = TRUE)
```

```{r growth-values, include = FALSE}
docket_year <- transform(docket, year = year_of(time),
                         per_tribunal = n_nodes / n_edges)
connected <- subset(docket_year, n_components == 1 & n_edges > 5)
widest <- head(subset(docket_year, diameter == max(diameter)), 1)
tightest <- head(subset(docket_year, per_tribunal == min(per_tribunal)), 1)
last_year <- tail(docket_year, 1)
```

At the inspected dates in
`r paste(connected$year, collapse = " and ")`, all active tribunals belong
to one component, involving up to `r max(connected$n_nodes)` arbitrators.
The largest reported diameter is `r widest$diameter` in
`r widest$year`; each graph step links arbitrators sharing an active
tribunal. At the last date, `r last_year$year`, there are
`r last_year$n_edges` active tribunals in `r last_year$n_components`
components.

The active-arbitrator count divided by active-tribunal count reaches
`r num(tightest$per_tribunal)` in `r tightest$year` and is
`r num(last_year$per_tribunal)` at the final date. A smaller ratio is
consistent with more shared memberships, but component structure and
the actual incidence are needed to describe how that overlap is arranged.

A tribunal's external neighbourhood consists of non-member
arbitrators connected to one of its members through another tribunal.
Summarise these neighbourhood sizes within each active snapshot.

```{r neighbourhood}
neighbourhood <- hg_edges(tribunals, what = "summary", measure = "n_neighbors",
                          at = grid)
```

```{r neighbourhood-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(neighbourhood, columns = c("mean", "q25", "median", "q75"),
     facets = FALSE)
```

```{r neighbourhood-values, include = FALSE}
largest_neighbourhood <- head(subset(neighbourhood, mean == max(mean)), 1)
```

The largest mean neighbourhood size is
`r num(largest_neighbourhood$mean, 1)` arbitrators in
`r year_of(largest_neighbourhood$time)`. The surrounding time series
shows whether this observation is isolated or part of a sustained change.

The storyline display follows the eight arbitrators with the largest
tribunal counts (Tanahashi and Ma 2012). Columns are ordered by tribunal
constitution, and a line spans an arbitrator's first and last displayed
tribunal. Grey bars mark common memberships. The layout brings frequently
co-occurring arbitrators closer together, and line width represents
appointment count. The lines do not represent continuous observation
or uninterrupted service between cases.

```{r storyline, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(tribunals, type = "storyline", spacing = "strength", width_by = "degree")
```

```{r storyline-values, include = FALSE}
storyline_seats <- unique(subset(argentina,
                                 select = c(arbitrator, case, constituted)))
eight <- head(hg_get(argentina_all, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree"), 8)
eight_seats <- subset(storyline_seats, arbitrator %in% eight$node)
together <- merge(eight_seats, eight_seats, by = c("case", "constituted"))
together <- subset(together, arbitrator.x < arbitrator.y)
shared <- aggregate(case ~ arbitrator.x + arbitrator.y, data = together,
                    FUN = length)
closest <- head(subset(shared, case == max(case)), 1)
apart <- setdiff(eight$node, c(shared$arbitrator.x, shared$arbitrator.y))
first_seat <- aggregate(constituted ~ arbitrator, data = eight_seats, FUN = min)
last_seat <- aggregate(constituted ~ arbitrator, data = eight_seats, FUN = max)
spans <- merge(first_seat, last_seat, by = "arbitrator",
               suffixes = c("_first", "_last"))
spans <- transform(spans, years = as.numeric(constituted_last -
                                               constituted_first) / 365.25)
longest <- head(subset(spans, years == max(years)), 1)
```

`r closest$arbitrator.x` and `r closest$arbitrator.y` share
`r closest$case` tribunals, the largest pair count among these eight
arbitrators. `r paste(apart, collapse = " and ")` shares no tribunal with
another member of the displayed subset. The longest displayed span is
for `r longest$arbitrator`, from
`r format(longest$constituted_first, "%Y")` to
`r format(longest$constituted_last, "%Y")`. These are summaries of the
selected appointments, rather than measures of the full careers.

## Which tribunals held the docket together

For s = 1, the line graph connects tribunals sharing an arbitrator.
Tribunal betweenness accumulates the fractions of shortest paths between
other tribunals passing through it. Computing this measure within each
snapshot identifies cases that connect concurrently active tribunal
groups under the shared-member definition.

```{r bridges}
bridges <- hg_edge_centrality(tribunals, s = 1, measure = "betweenness",
                              at = grid, top = 1)
bridges
```

```{r bridges-values, include = FALSE}
bridging <- subset(bridges, value > 0)
first_quiet <- min(subset(bridges, value == 0 & time > as.Date("2010-01-01"))$time)
```

Across the grid, `r length(unique(bridging$edge))` tribunals attain
the largest betweenness at least once. From
`r format(first_quiet, "%Y")`, the inspected snapshots have no active
tribunal with positive intermediary betweenness. Check the line-graph
structure before attributing a zero score to one cause: it can occur in
isolated or directly connected groups as well as fully disconnected data.

```{r peak-values, include = FALSE}
busiest <- head(subset(docket, n_edges == max(n_edges)), 1)
```

The largest active docket on this grid occurs in
`r year_of(busiest$time)`, with `r busiest$n_edges` tribunals.
For a closer view, select the ten highest-betweenness tribunals in the
snapshot dated 1 June 2006 (Aksoy et al. 2020). This is a ranked subset
of the snapshot, rather than a formally defined network backbone.

```{r backbone}
peak <- hg_snapshot(tribunals, at = as.Date("2006-06-01"))
backbone_cases <- hg_edge_centrality(peak, s = 1, measure = "betweenness",
                                     top = 10)
backbone <- hg_subset(peak, edges = backbone_cases)
```

```{r backbone-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
plot(backbone, color_by = "economic_sector", legend_title = "economic sector")
```

```{r backbone-values, include = FALSE}
hub <- hg_get(backbone, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree", top = 1)
backbone_sectors <- length(unique(hg_get(backbone, what = "edge_data")$economic_sector))
```

The selected date contains `r peak$n_hyperedges` active tribunals.
The top-ten subset covers `r backbone_sectors` economic sectors, and
`r hub$node` appears on `r hub$degree` of its tribunals. The economic
sector colours help describe the selected cases without affecting
their betweenness ranking.

Compare this with closeness calculated on the aggregate of all
tribunals. Aggregate paths can connect cases that were never concurrently
active, so this ranking describes a different relation from snapshot
closeness.

```{r anachronism}
aggregate_cases <- hg_edge_centrality(argentina_all, s = 1,
                                      measure = "closeness", top = 10)
aggregate_cases
```

```{r anachronism-values, include = FALSE}
spans <- subset(hg_get(argentina_all, what = "edge_data"),
                edge %in% aggregate_cases$edge, select = c(edge, start, end))
spans <- transform(spans, end = ifelse(is.na(end), end_offset, end))
together <- outer(spans$start, spans$end, "<=") &
  outer(spans$end, spans$start, ">=")
apart_pairs <- sum(!together) / 2
all_pairs <- choose(nrow(spans), 2)
```

Among the `r all_pairs` pairs in the selected aggregate top ten,
`r apart_pairs` have no overlap in their case intervals. Aggregation
retains their shared-arbitrator relations while removing the constraint
of concurrent activity. Choose the aggregate or snapshot analysis
according to whether the research question concerns appointment history
or concurrent structure.

The following table reports aggregate betweenness for comparison
with the snapshot ranking.

```{r aggregate-betweenness}
aggregate_bridges <- hg_edge_centrality(argentina_all, s = 1,
                                        measure = "betweenness", top = 10)
aggregate_bridges
```

```{r aggregate-betweenness-values, include = FALSE}
n_both <- length(intersect(aggregate_bridges$edge, aggregate_cases$edge))
```

The aggregate top-ten betweenness and closeness lists share
`r n_both` tribunals. Plot the highest-betweenness subset by economic
sector to inspect its membership structure.

```{r aggregate-central}
central_tribunals <- hg_subset(argentina_all, edges = aggregate_bridges)
```

```{r aggregate-central-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
plot(central_tribunals, color_by = "economic_sector",
     legend_title = "economic sector")
```

```{r aggregate-central-values, include = FALSE}
central_hub <- hg_get(central_tribunals, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree",
                      top = 1)
```

Within this selected subset, `r central_hub$node` appears on
`r central_hub$degree` tribunals. Shared membership helps explain the
displayed connectivity, but the aggregate still includes nonconcurrent
appointments.

## Communities of arbitrators

Compare two community objectives on the aggregate. IRMM iterates
weighted clique projection, Louvain partitioning, and hyperedge
reweighting (Kumar et al. 2020). Infomap partitions the association
projection by minimising random-walk description length (Rosvall and
Bergstrom 2008). Each method uses 20 seeds. Its medoid is the run with
greatest summed adjusted mutual information with the other runs.
Hypergraph modularity subsequently scores the partitions using
majority-based hyperedge contributions (Kamiński et al. 2019).

```{r communities}
irmm <- hg_communities(argentina_all, type = "irmm", seeds = 1:20,
                       n_runs = 20, max_iter = 300)
hg_modularity(argentina_all, irmm)
infomap <- hg_communities(argentina_all, seeds = 1:20, n_runs = 20)
hg_modularity(argentina_all, infomap)
hg_agreement(irmm, infomap, method = c("ari", "ami"))
```

```{r communities-values, include = FALSE}
irmm_sizes <- hg_get(irmm, what = "sizes")
irmm_ami <- hg_get(irmm, what = "ami")
irmm_modularity <- hg_modularity(argentina_all, irmm)
infomap_sizes <- hg_get(infomap, what = "sizes")
infomap_modularity <- hg_modularity(argentina_all, infomap)
infomap_ami <- hg_get(infomap, what = "ami")
partition_agreement <- hg_agreement(irmm, infomap, method = c("ari", "ami"))
```

The IRMM medoid has `r nrow(irmm_sizes)` communities, sizes from
`r min(irmm_sizes$n_nodes)` to `r max(irmm_sizes$n_nodes)`, and
hypergraph modularity `r num(irmm_modularity$modularity, 3)`.
Median agreement across its runs is `r num(median(irmm_ami$ami))`.
The Infomap medoid has `r nrow(infomap_sizes)` communities, modularity
`r num(infomap_modularity$modularity, 3)`, and median run agreement
`r num(median(infomap_ami$ami))`. Between the medoids, the adjusted Rand
index is `r num(partition_agreement$ari)` and adjusted mutual information
is `r num(partition_agreement$ami)`. The plot applies IRMM labels to
the previously selected top-ten snapshot tribunals.

```{r communities-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
plot(backbone, node_groups = irmm)
```

Inspect the per-community decomposition to identify the observed
and reference contributions underlying the IRMM partition's total
hypergraph modularity.

```{r modularity-communities}
hg_modularity(argentina_all, irmm, what = "communities")
```

```{r modularity-communities-values, include = FALSE}
by_community <- hg_modularity(argentina_all, irmm, what = "communities")
top_community <- head(subset(by_community, modularity == max(modularity)), 1)
lone_tribunals <- subset(by_community, n_nodes == 3L & volume == 3)
```

The community containing `r top_community$n_nodes` arbitrators makes
the largest contribution, `r num(top_community$modularity, 3)`, to total
modularity `r num(irmm_modularity$modularity, 3)`.
There are `r nrow(lone_tribunals)` communities of three arbitrators and
weighted degree volume three. Compare their member sets with the observed
panels to determine whether each community corresponds to a single tribunal.

## Argentina and the other cases

The table brings together the descriptive comparisons made above.
Concentration, repetition, assortativity, and null-model deviations
measure different aspects of tribunal membership. Their denominators
and reference distributions differ between subsets. A comparative
inferential analysis would need to specify a common estimand and
account for those differences.

```{r comparison, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  measure = c("tribunals", "arbitrators",
              "share of seats held by the ten busiest arbitrators",
              "share of tribunals that repeat a panel",
              "degree assortativity",
              "repeated panels, z against the swap null"),
  argentina = c(rep_value("mh", "n_edges"), rep_value("mh", "n_nodes"),
                pct(argentina_top), pct(repeat_share), num(assort_argentina),
                num(test_value(repeats_swap, "repeated_edges", "z"), 1)),
  other = c(rep_value("mh", "n_edges", other_reps),
            rep_value("mh", "n_nodes", other_reps),
            pct(other_top), pct(other_repeat_share), num(assort_other),
            num(test_value(repeats_other, "repeated_edges", "z"), 1))
), col.names = c("", "claims against Argentina", "cases against other states"))
```
